Since the middle of the twentieth century it has appeared in teaching and research at schools, conservatories and the Sibelius Academy, in traditional, Western classical and electronic music. Early instruments had five or six horsehair strings on a body of a single piece of wood; later came metal strings and bodies of several pieces. In the 1920s Paul Salminen introduced the semitone switch, which led to concert models with up to 40 strings. From the middle of the twentieth century players such as Martti Pokela drove its development, teaching entered schools and the Sibelius Academy, electric versions appeared, and the instrument entered heavy metal and studio composition.

The kantele (also kannel) is a traditional plucked instrument of Finland and Karelia, a box zither of the Baltic psaltery family along with the Estonian kannel, the Latvian kokles, the Lithuanian kanklės and the Russian gusli, H-S number 314.122-5. Small instruments mostly have fewer than fifteen strings, and the traditional form has no bridge and no nut, the strings running from the pegs straight to a metal bar in a wooden holder; it is played resting on the knees or a small table, plucked or strummed with the fingers. It can be used for solo playing and in folk ensembles, while concert models are used in modern performance and teaching.
演奏者將坎泰萊琴置於膝上或小桌上，以手指撥弦，或以未按住的弦掃弦，有時使用火柴棒: The player rests the kantele on the knees or a small table and plucks the strings with the fingers, or strums across the strings that are not stopped, sometimes using a matchstick. A beginner can first learn the traditional tuning of the five-string small kantele, usually D major or D minor in five-limit just intonation, and use the semitone lever to switch between F♯1 and F1, so that most folk tunes can be played without retuning.
